demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is a physical therapist, forty-three years old, and she has not touched a resistance band in four months without seeing the ceiling tiles first. The memory starts with the ceiling tiles-the way they caught the fluorescent light, the one with the water stain near the vent-because that is what she looked at while she waited for the code team to arrive. She had been working with a patient named Malcolm, a sixty-seven-year-old retired fisherman with a new hip replacement. He was strong, stubborn, and liked to joke about the rain. On that Tuesday afternoon, she was guiding him through a standing transfer from the treatment table to his walker. He was unsteady, but that was typical post-op. She placed her hand on his lower back, felt him shift his weight, and then he was falling. She tried to catch him, but her foot slipped on a gel pad, and she pulled him sideways instead of breaking his fall. His head hit the corner of the handrail. The sound was wet and sharp. He stopped moving.

She remembers screaming for help. She remembers holding his head, telling him it would be okay, while blood spread through her fingers. He survived the surgery for the subdural hematoma, but he has not spoken, eaten, or opened his eyes since. He is in a long-term care facility three miles from the clinic. She has never visited him. She cannot drive past the building.

Now, in the present, she wakes at 3:47 a.m. most mornings, her heart pounding so hard that her partner, a high school art teacher named Leilani, reaches for her in the dark. She does not tell Leilani what she saw in the dream-Malcolm's face, the blood, the ceiling tiles-because saying it out loud makes it real. Instead, she lies still and replays the fall frame by frame, trying to find the second where she could have done something different. She never finds it.

At work, she is a ghost of the therapist she was. She used to specialize in post-surgical rehab, but now she requests only chronic pain patients who do not need transfers or gait training. When a new patient with a hip replacement is scheduled on her caseload, she asks a colleague to swap. She does not explain why. She avoids the treatment table near the handrail where Malcolm fell. She has rearranged her treatment room twice so she does not have to see that corner. Her hands shake when she demonstrates balance exercises. She has started leaving the door open during sessions, a habit she cannot explain to herself. She checks the emergency stop button three times before each patient.

She has become quiet at home. Leilani says she is distant, that she flinches when touched unexpectedly. She has stopped going to the beach on weekends-the smell of salt water reminds her of the antiseptic in the hospital hallway. She has stopped cooking, because she cannot stand the sound of a knife on a cutting board. She spends evenings sitting on the couch, not reading, not watching television, just staring at the wall. She tells herself she is resting. She knows she is avoiding her own mind.

At their last session, she sat with her hands folded in her lap, her voice flat, and said, "I used to think I was good at my job. I used to think I helped people. Now I just look at the ceiling tiles every time I walk into a room." She did not cry. She has not cried since the accident. She cannot remember the last time she felt anything except the weight of her own chest pressing down on her lungs. She is still going to work. She is still coming home. She is still breathing. But she is not sure, anymore, that she is really here.
